evidence.field: Old Chinese pronunciation of 床/牀
evidence.text: The opened entry lists the Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese reconstruction for the bed word written 床 as *zraŋ. It separately lists Mandarin chuáng and Middle Chinese dzrjang; these are different periods and transcription systems.
evidence.title: 床 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.text: In its Zhengzhang (2003) phonetic-series table, the entry lists 爿 with *zaŋ, alongside *braːn as an additional reconstruction. The source therefore does not give only *zraŋ for 爿. The table lists 床/牀 as *zraŋ. This supports a same-system comparison of the entries, but not a claim that 爿’s independently reconstructed pronunciation was *zraŋ.
evidence.title: 爿 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.field: 牀 phonetic-series analysis and pronunciation comparison
evidence.text: The opened entry labels 爿 as the phonetic component and 木 as semantic in 牀. Its table of characters in the 爿 phonetic series attributes Zhengzhang (2003) forms *zaŋ (also *braːn) to 爿 and *zraŋ to 牀. This is secondary presentation of the reconstruction and component analysis, not direct confirmation from Zhengzhang’s published source.

search_audit.outcome: Search found a 爿 entry and the CUHK paleographic entry. Opened the Wiktionary page and inspected its Zhengzhang phonetic-series table; it lists 爿 as *zaŋ (also *braːn) and 床/牀 as *zraŋ.

search_audit.query: Zhengzhang reconstruction 爿 牀 Old Chinese
search_audit.outcome: Search returned a Zhengzhang data module and character entries. Opening the data module returned an internal error; opened the English 牀 entry and inspected its phonetic-series table, which supplies the same comparison as the Chinese entry.

gaps: The inspected pages attribute the reconstructions to Zhengzhang (2003), but are secondary sources; this search did not verify the pair against Zhengzhang’s original publication or a direct authoritative reconstruction database.

The same-system values are not identical as listed: 爿 has *zaŋ (and an additional *braːn), while 床/牀 has *zraŋ. The phonetic-series relationship is reported by the source, but these entries alone do not establish the sound history or exact phonetic fit.

No new primary paleographic evidence was inspected in this focused source check. The dossier’s cited account that 爿 served as a phonetic element in 牀 remains a historical source assertion; uncertainty about the early depicted referent or name of 爿 is separate from this pronunciation comparison.
